name: MutationObserver semantics and its blind spots. Canonical name: MutationObserver, defined in WHATWG DOM Standard section 4.3 (Mutation observers), with MutationRecord, MutationObserverInit, the queue-a-mutation-record algorithm, registered and TRANSIENT registered observers, and the notify-mutation-observers microtask. Predecessor: DOM Level 3 Mutation Events (DOMSubtreeModified, DOMNodeInserted and family), deprecated for performance and reentrancy reasons and replaced by MutationObserver in 2012. Sibling observers that cover parts of what it does not: IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver, PerformanceObserver, the slotchange event, and the still-unspecified ComputedStyleObserver/StyleObserver that the CSS WG has an open issue for and browsers do not ship.
kind: Browser feature defined by a living standard (WHATWG DOM). Not a library, benchmark or service. Evaluated here as the mechanism the project's O(delta) claim rests on, so the question is not what it does but precisely what it does NOT report.
maturity: Production and universally shipped since roughly 2012-2013 across Chromium, Gecko and WebKit; part of a living standard, so semantics can in principle change but the core has been stable for over a decade. Mutation Events, the predecessor, are removed or removal-in-progress in modern engines, so MutationObserver is the only supported synchronous-ish DOM change channel. There is an open WHATWG DOM issue (whatwg/dom#1340) proposing observation of element PROPERTIES such as input.value and checkbox.checked; it is not implemented anywhere, which means the property blind spot below is a permanent feature of the current platform rather than a temporary gap.
license: A browser API defined by a royalty-free living standard; no licence obstacle of any kind. The WHATWG standard text is CC-BY-4.0. Free to use here.
keeps_and_discards: MutationObserver reports exactly three classes of change to the NODE TREE and nothing else: childList (children added or removed from a target), attributes (an attribute set or removed on an element), and characterData (the data of a CharacterData node changed). It keeps node references for added and removed nodes, the previousSibling and nextSibling at the time of removal, the attribute name and namespace, and -- only if explicitly requested via attributeOldValue or characterDataOldValue -- the previous value. It discards the previous CONTENT of anything removed (you get live node references, whose contents can be further mutated after removal, so a record is not a snapshot), it discards intermediate states within a microtask, and it discards any notion of 'move' -- a relocated node is reported as a removal plus an addition with nothing linking them. Everything below in delta_cost_model and failure_modes is a consequence of the fact that the node tree is only one of at least six mutable state spaces a page has, and MutationObserver watches one of them.
structure_preserved: Records preserve enough to reconstruct the node-tree edit: target, type, added/removed node lists, and the sibling pair bracketing a removal, which together determine insertion position exactly. Order is therefore recoverable. Nesting is recoverable only by walking the added or removed nodes -- a childList record for an innerHTML replacement reports ONE record with N removed and M added top-level nodes, and the entire subtree beneath each is implicit, so reconstructing the structural delta requires an O(subtree) walk that the record itself does not pay for. Tabular relations are not represented; a table is just nodes. SHADOW BOUNDARIES ARE THE CENTRAL STRUCTURAL BLIND SPOT and deserve to be stated exactly: a shadow root is the root of a SEPARATE node tree, not a descendant of its host in the node tree, so observe(host, {subtree: true}) does NOT report mutations inside host's shadow root. Each shadow root must be observed separately with its own observe() call on the ShadowRoot node. Consequently the composed tree -- the thing the project actually folds -- has no single observer; it has one observer per shadow root, and the set of shadow roots is itself a moving target that must be discovered and re-discovered.
interactive_elements: Controls are observed only as elements, and only their ATTRIBUTES are observed. This is the most operationally damaging blind spot for a tag-plus-interactivity design and it is worth being blunt about: the IDL properties that carry a control's actual state are not attributes and generate no records. input.value set by script, or typed by a user, does not change the value content attribute and produces NO mutation record. A checkbox's checkedness likewise diverges from the checked attribute after the first user interaction or scripted assignment (the attribute is the DEFAULT, the property is the state) and produces no record. Same for select.selectedIndex and an option's selectedness, input.indeterminate, input.files, textarea.value, the dirty-value flag generally, and form validity state. A page whose entire visible change is 'the user checked three boxes and the submit button became enabled' produces exactly one mutation record -- the disabled attribute removal -- and the three checkbox states are invisible. Detecting them requires either polling the properties or listening to input/change/click events, and events do not fire for programmatic assignment, so neither route is complete. WHATWG DOM issue 1340 exists precisely because there is no correct solution today.
interactive_state_fidelity: Attribute-reflected state is reported faithfully and cheaply: disabled, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-checked, open on details/dialog, hidden, and any data-* or class-driven state all arrive as attribute records with optional old values, and attributeFilter keeps the cost proportional to the attributes you care about. Property-backed state is not reported at all, per above. The practical consequence is that a design relying on MutationObserver has HIGH fidelity for author-declared state (ARIA and attributes, which is what a well-built component uses) and ZERO fidelity for user-interaction state on native form controls. Since ARIA attributes are exactly the ones a component library updates when it expands a menu or selects a tab, the coverage is better than it first appears for framework-built UI and worse than it appears for plain HTML forms. Token cost of carrying the observed state is negligible -- an attribute record is a name plus two short strings -- and using attributeFilter to restrict to the interactivity-relevant attribute set (aria-*, disabled, checked, selected, open, hidden, href, role, tabindex, contenteditable, style, class) is the correct economy, at the cost of losing old-value coverage for anything outside the filter.
layout_awareness: None whatsoever, which is simultaneously the constraint-clean property and the biggest soundness hole. MutationObserver never reads geometry, never triggers layout, and cannot be used to detect a visual change. That means it satisfies no_layout_in_the_fold trivially. It also means an enormous class of user-visible change is invisible to it -- see delta_cost_model. The platform's answer for geometry is ResizeObserver and IntersectionObserver, which DO consume layout and therefore belong, in this project's terms, strictly in the actuator layer alongside the ASCII wireframe.
javascript_required: The observer itself is JavaScript running in the page's event loop (or an extension's isolated world sharing the same loop), so yes by construction. More consequentially, its coverage begins only when observe() is called: everything that happened before registration is unrecoverable from records and must be obtained by an initial full walk. For a streamed HTML document the parser inserts nodes progressively, so an observer registered at DOMContentLoaded has missed the entire document and an observer registered at document_start in an extension catches the parse as a long stream of childList records -- a genuine choice with different cost profiles, and the second one turns initial load into the single largest delta the system will ever process.
evaluation_method: Correctness of the API is established by the WHATWG DOM specification's algorithms plus web-platform-tests, which is the strongest form of evaluation available for a browser feature: an executable conformance suite run by all three engines, independent of any one vendor. What is NOT evaluated anywhere is the property this project needs -- COMPLETENESS with respect to user-visible change. No specification, test suite or study claims that mutation records cover everything a user could perceive, and the correct reading of the spec is that it explicitly does not: it covers the node tree, and says so. For the project, the right evaluation method is a differential one that does not exist in the literature and would have to be built: capture a page's fold, drive an interaction, apply the observed delta to the stored fold, then independently re-capture the page in full and diff the two folds. Any difference is a blind spot, and the diff names it. That is an oracle-free soundness test for the O(delta) claim and it is the single most valuable experiment implied by this item.
corpus_size_and_origins: Not applicable in the usual sense -- there is no evaluation corpus for a browser API. web-platform-tests covers the API's own semantics on synthetic documents, not real pages. The relevant reach limitation is different and worth recording: all practitioner knowledge about MutationObserver blind spots comes from bug reports, Stack Overflow threads and standards issues (whatwg/dom#1340, the CSS Houdini ComputedStyleObserver request w3c/css-houdini-drafts#987, the WICG style-observer discussions), which is anecdote aggregated over an unknown population of pages. Nobody has published a measurement of what FRACTION of user-visible change on real pages is invisible to MutationObserver, on any corpus. That number does not exist and the project would be the first to have it.
reported_precision_recall: No such figures exist and none are meaningful for a specification. The figures that WOULD matter and are unpublished: (a) the fraction of user-visible page changes on real pages that produce zero mutation records; (b) the record-count amplification factor, i.e. records emitted per unit of net semantic change, which on framework-driven pages is routinely far above one because virtual-DOM reconciliation and CSS-in-JS churn produce large numbers of records with no net effect; (c) the fraction of pages using closed shadow roots, where observation is impossible by design. All three are directly measurable on the project's own 136-page corpus and none is available from the literature. [uncertain] on all quantities in this field, because there are none.
independent_oracle: Yes, and it is cheap and decisive: a full re-capture. The observer's claim is 'the stored state plus these records equals the current state'; a fresh full walk of the composed tree tests exactly that claim using a mechanism that shares no assumptions with the record stream. Running it periodically -- every Nth interaction, or on a timer -- converts the O(delta) guarantee from an assertion into a continuously falsified hypothesis, and the diff localises the blind spot to a specific address. This is the strongest available answer to the project's stated need to make the guarantee falsifiable, and it is the recommendation to adopt. A second, weaker oracle is a per-node Merkle hash: comparing a stored subtree root hash against a freshly computed one detects drift without a full diff, at the cost of a walk.
evidence_independence: The specification is a multi-vendor consensus document, so it is as close to vendor-neutral as browser evidence gets, and web-platform-tests results are cross-engine and public. The blind-spot catalogue below is assembled from the spec's own scope statements plus standards-issue discussion, not from any vendor's marketing, so there is nothing here to launder. The one thing that should be flagged as NOT independently established is any claim about the PERFORMANCE of MutationObserver at high mutation rates; the available statements are engine-implementer assertions and microbenchmarks, and the project should measure on its own workload rather than cite them.
page_archetype_coverage: Varies enormously and predictably. Documentation and article pages are near-static after load, so the record stream is nearly empty and O(delta) is trivially satisfied. Listing, feed and product pages using virtualised scrolling produce continuous, high-volume childList churn where recycled rows are removed and re-added constantly -- delta approaches page size per scroll event, and the observer reports a torrent of records for what a human perceives as one continuous scroll. Forum and chat pages append steadily, which is the ideal case: small, genuinely incremental deltas. Application-shell and dashboard pages built on component frameworks generate attribute and class churn from CSS-in-JS and state libraries at rates far exceeding semantic change. Service and checkout flows are the worst case for the property blind spot, because the meaningful state lives entirely in form-control properties that generate no records at all. Any aggregate 'MutationObserver is O(delta)' claim conceals this spread the same way a single extraction F-score conceals WCXB's 0.93-to-0.41 range.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Script- and locale-invariant, genuinely and for a good reason: the API operates on node identity and attribute names, not on text semantics. characterData records carry the full new data string and, optionally, the old, with no tokenisation, segmentation or normalisation of any kind, so CJK, RTL and whitespace-free scripts are handled identically to Latin. Two caveats. First, characterData records give you the whole new value, not a character-level diff, so a one-character edit in a large text node costs the whole node -- a delta-amplification issue that is language-neutral but interacts with script, since CJK text nodes carry more content per character. Second, any downstream diffing of characterData values must normalise Unicode consistently or the same visible text in NFC and NFD registers as a change; the observer will faithfully report a real data change, and the false positive is the consumer's fault, not the API's.
leaks_outward: The observer discloses nothing to the network. It discloses nothing to the page directly either -- registration is not visible from script, and there is no API to enumerate observers on a node. What it CAN leak is second-order: the callback runs as a microtask in the same event loop as the page, so heavy observer work lengthens tasks and delays the page's own timers and rAF callbacks, a timing side channel the page can measure. A page that instruments requestAnimationFrame intervals or uses PerformanceObserver on longtask entries can detect that something expensive is running in response to its DOM churn, and can amplify the signal deliberately by mutating heavily and measuring the induced jitter. This is a real detection avenue for a covert sensor and is under-discussed.
mechanism_detectability: Passive observation is not directly detectable -- this is the API's key advantage over the alternatives and the reason it, rather than attachShadow patching or CDP, should carry the delta channel. Contrast: patching attachShadow is trivially detectable by Function.prototype.toString inspection or by comparing against a fresh iframe's realm, and is refused by the project's constraints; enabling CDP Runtime has its own known detection surface. MutationObserver has none of that. The residual detectability surfaces are three and all are avoidable. (1) The timing channel above -- mitigate by doing minimal work in the callback and deferring processing off the critical path, and by using takeRecords() to drain rather than doing expensive work synchronously. (2) ANY DOM MUTATION THE SENSOR PERFORMS is visible to the page's own MutationObserver, so the sensor must be strictly read-only; injecting markers, wrapping text nodes for highlighting, or setting data attributes as bookkeeping are all self-reporting and must not be done. (3) Registering an observer on a node makes that node's removal produce a TRANSIENT registered observer, which is spec-internal and not script-visible, so it leaks nothing -- worth noting only because it is sometimes wrongly assumed to be observable.
countermeasures: For the project as observer, the hardening is: stay read-only; use attributeFilter to bound both cost and the observer's own footprint; drain with takeRecords() and process asynchronously to flatten the timing signature; never patch a platform function. For the project as a system that must not be fooled: a page can DEFEAT delta tracking cheaply and there is no countermeasure within the API, only detection. Specifically a page can put content in a closed shadow root (unobservable, and the project correctly refuses the patch that would reach it), render text via CSS generated content (unobservable), draw to canvas (unobservable), or churn the DOM at high rates to bury real changes in noise. The only real countermeasure is the periodic full re-capture oracle, which converts every one of these from an invisible failure into a measured discrepancy.
measured_fidelity_cost: Unmeasured in the literature and directly measurable here. The specific quantity: fold-after-delta versus fold-after-full-recapture, expressed as the fraction of nodes and characters that differ, on the project's own 136-page corpus, per archetype. Against the control of a full recapture on every interaction, the cost of delta-only tracking is exactly that discrepancy, and it will not be zero. A second measurable: the cost of restricting attributeFilter, which trades completeness for volume and whose loss is enumerable by running with and without the filter on the same session.
gate_state_at_capture: Not represented; MutationObserver has no concept of a document's provenance or access state. Relevant indirectly in one way that matters: consent banners, paywall interstitials and login walls are themselves DOM, and their appearance and dismissal generate mutation records like anything else, so the gate state is INFERABLE from the record stream but only by a heuristic that names a region -- which the project's structure_agnosticism constraint forbids. Gate state must therefore be recorded out of band at capture time (HTTP status, cookie presence, an explicit operator annotation), not derived from mutations.
determinism: The API is deterministic in what it reports for a given sequence of DOM operations: the queue-a-mutation-record algorithm is fully specified and the record contents are a pure function of the mutation. It is NOT deterministic in delivery timing relative to the page's own code, because records are delivered in a microtask checkpoint and multiple mutations coalesce into one callback invocation with a batch of records -- so how many callbacks you get, and how many records per callback, depends on how the page's synchronous work happens to be sliced. Two runs of the same page can therefore produce identical record SEQUENCES with different BATCHING, and any consumer whose behaviour depends on batch boundaries is non-deterministic. Additional non-determinism sources: mutations produced by the page's own timers, animations, network responses and intersection callbacks are wall-clock dependent, so a live page is never deterministic regardless of the API. One under-appreciated exactness detail: setting an attribute to its EXISTING value still queues a record -- the spec's change-an-attribute path does not short-circuit on equality -- so a page that re-sets className to the same string every frame produces a full record stream with zero semantic change. That is an amplification, not a blind spot, and it means record count is a poor proxy for change magnitude.
determinism_across_versions: The record semantics are stable and cross-engine, backed by web-platform-tests, so the API contract does not drift meaningfully. What drifts underneath it is the DOM the records describe: HTML parser behaviour (whitespace text nodes, implied tbody, template and slot handling, error recovery), custom-element upgrade timing, and framework hydration strategies all change what nodes exist and therefore what records are produced for the same page across browser builds. Microtask timing relative to rendering has also been tightened over the years. Newer platform additions change the record stream too -- most notably the state-preserving atomic move API (moveBefore), which changes how a relocation is represented compared with the classic remove-then-insert pair, so consumers that assume every relocation appears as a remove/add pair may behave differently on engines that have it. [uncertain] on the precise mutation-record shape produced by moveBefore across engines; this should be verified directly in the target browser rather than assumed.
reproducibility: The API is reproducible; the pages are not. Replaying a stored record stream against a stored initial DOM is fully reproducible and is the right way to build a regression test for the fold. Re-deriving the same record stream from a live page is not reproducible for the same reason the project's corpus is not frozen -- 75% of its pages fetch live resources on every read, and every one of those fetches produces different mutations. The actionable conclusion: record the mutation stream as a first-class artifact alongside the initial capture, so a fold can be recomputed offline from frozen inputs. That artifact is also what makes the blind-spot oracle repeatable.
failure_modes: The blind-spot catalogue, which is this item's main deliverable. Each entry is a class of change that produces NO mutation record. (1) SHADOW ROOTS NOT INDIVIDUALLY OBSERVED. A shadow root is a separate tree; subtree:true on the host does not reach into it. Every open shadow root needs its own observe() call, and newly attached shadow roots need discovering -- the attachShadow call itself produces no record, so a shadow root created after registration is invisible until something else reveals it. Closed shadow roots cannot be observed at all, and the project refuses the patch that would change that, so content inside closed roots is permanently outside the delta channel and must be declared as such. (2) DECLARATIVE SHADOW DOM IN THE INITIAL PARSE. A template with shadowrootmode is converted by the HTML parser into a ShadowRoot at parse time, before any script-registered observer exists for it; the content never generates records and, because the template element is replaced by the shadow root, there is no element left whose insertion would hint at it. Server-rendered web-component pages therefore deliver a substantial fraction of their content entirely outside the record stream. This must be handled by an initial walk that enumerates shadow roots, and re-enumeration is needed whenever new hosts appear. (3) CSS-DRIVEN VISUAL CHANGE. Nothing in the style pipeline produces mutation records: a media-query or container-query response, a :hover/:focus/:checked selector match, a CSS transition or animation, a stylesheet swap's downstream effect on thousands of elements, display:none appearing or disappearing because a class matched differently. Note the asymmetry -- the class attribute change IS reported, the thousands of computed-style changes it causes are not, so the sensor sees the cause and not the effect. There is no ComputedStyleObserver; the CSS WG has an open request (w3c/css-houdini-drafts#987) and browsers do not ship one, and the only working technique in the wild is Bramus's style-observer, which abuses CSS transitions plus transitionrun events to get a push notification for a declared property list -- clever, bounded to properties you name in advance, and not something the platform guarantees. (4) CSS GENERATED CONTENT. Text produced by ::before/::after content, list markers, and CSS counters is USER-VISIBLE TEXT THAT IS NOT IN THE DOM AT ALL. It is not merely unobservable as a change; it is absent from any DOM-based fold, delta or otherwise. This is a fidelity hole as much as a delta hole and it is worth stating separately because a full re-capture does not fix it either. (5) CSSOM MUTATION. sheet.insertRule/deleteRule, changes to adoptedStyleSheets, and constructable stylesheet edits mutate style without touching the node tree. Note the contrast with element.style.setProperty, which DOES reflect into the style content attribute and therefore IS reported. (6) FORM-CONTROL PROPERTY STATE, as detailed above: value, checkedness, selectedness, indeterminate, files, dirty flags. Invisible, and there is no proposed-and-shipped fix. (7) CANVAS, VIDEO, WEBGL AND IMAGE CONTENT. Drawing into a canvas, decoding a new video frame, or an img's pixels changing after its src attribute mutation are all invisible; only the attribute change is seen, never the content. (8) IFRAME CONTENT. A nested browsing context is a separate document needing its own observer, obtainable only for same-origin frames; cross-origin frames are wholly opaque and their content is outside both the fold and the delta by browser policy. (9) SLOT REASSIGNMENT. Changing which nodes are assigned to which slot changes the FLATTENED tree without changing the node tree -- the platform signals this with a slotchange event, not a mutation record. Since the project folds the COMPOSED tree, this is a direct soundness hole: the composed tree can change with an empty record stream. slotchange must be listened for separately, per slot. (10) SCROLL, FOCUS, SELECTION, HOVER AND DIALOG/POPOVER TOP-LAYER STATE. None are node-tree changes. (11) PRE-REGISTRATION CHANGES. Anything before observe() is unrecoverable from records. (12) UNRETRIEVED RECORDS ON DISCONNECT. Calling disconnect() empties the record queue; pending records are lost unless takeRecords() is called first. (13) DETACHED-NODE READS. Removed nodes are delivered as live references, so if the page continues mutating them the record no longer describes what was removed -- a record is a pointer, not a snapshot, and reading it late reads a different thing. (14) QUEUE GROWTH UNDER LONG TASKS. Records accumulate without bound while the callback cannot run, so a page performing heavy synchronous DOM work delivers a very large batch at once, which is a memory and latency spike rather than a smooth stream.
failure_visibility: Silent across the board, and that is the defining problem. Every blind spot in the list above manifests as an absence -- no error, no warning, no signal of any kind. A fold that has silently diverged from the page looks exactly like a fold that is correct. There is no in-band way to detect divergence; detection requires the out-of-band oracle (periodic full re-capture, or subtree hash comparison). Given that the project explicitly refuses silent degradation, the correct posture is to treat every item in the failure_modes list as a NAMED, DECLARED exception carried in the capture metadata -- record per capture whether closed shadow roots were encountered, whether any canvas or cross-origin iframe elements exist, whether declarative shadow DOM was present, whether CSS generated content is in use -- so that a fold advertises its own known incompleteness rather than implying completeness it does not have. That list of flags is cheap to compute during the initial walk and turns an invisible hole into a visible caveat.
scale_limits: Cost is linear in RECORD COUNT, not in semantic change, and the two diverge badly. Superlinear regions: (a) subtree operations, where one record describing an innerHTML replacement obliges an O(subtree) walk to understand it, so record count stays at one while work is unbounded; (b) high-frequency churn from virtualised lists and animation-driven class toggling, where record volume is proportional to frame rate times list length; (c) callback backpressure, where a slow consumer lets the queue grow and the batch arrives as a spike; (d) the number of shadow roots, since each requires its own observer and observer registration is per-tree, so a page composed of thousands of web components carries thousands of registrations, each with fixed overhead. attributeFilter is the single most effective bound available and should be considered mandatory rather than an optimisation.
delta_cost_model: MutationObserver gives a per-change cost for node-tree changes only, and the honest statement of it is: cost is O(records) plus O(size of any added or removed subtree), where records is the number of DOM operations the page performed, NOT the size of the net semantic difference. What falls OUTSIDE the per-change cost, stated so the O(delta) claim is falsifiable: (1) SUBTREE ADD/REMOVE, where a single record obliges a walk proportional to the subtree, so a one-record delta can cost as much as a full page -- an innerHTML swap of a page's main region is one record and a whole-page cost; (2) CHARACTERDATA GRANULARITY, where a one-character edit delivers the entire new node value, so cost is proportional to the text node's size rather than the edit's; (3) NO-OP RECORDS, since setting an attribute to its existing value still queues a record, so a framework re-rendering identical class strings every frame produces a record stream with zero information content; (4) INITIAL LOAD, which is not a delta at all -- either a full walk or the entire parse arriving as records; (5) SHADOW-ROOT DISCOVERY, which requires walking to find new hosts because attachShadow produces no record, so the cost of staying correct about shadow roots is a periodic O(page) scan unless a cheaper trigger is found (observing childList and checking only newly-added elements for shadowRoot is the bounded approximation, and it misses shadow roots attached later to pre-existing elements); (6) DECLARATIVE SHADOW DOM in the initial parse, which never enters the record stream at all; (7) SLOT REASSIGNMENT, which changes the composed tree with no record, so the composed-tree delta is not bounded by the node-tree delta and slotchange must be observed separately; (8) ALL CSS-DRIVEN CHANGE -- computed style, media/container query response, transitions, pseudo-element generated content -- which is outside the model entirely and for which no push-based platform mechanism exists; (9) CANVAS, VIDEO, WEBGL and decoded image content, outside the model entirely; (10) FORM-CONTROL PROPERTY STATE, outside the model entirely; (11) CROSS-ORIGIN IFRAME content, outside by policy; (12) CLOSED SHADOW ROOTS, outside by design and by the project's own constraint; (13) the PERIODIC FULL RE-CAPTURE that soundness requires, which is O(page) by construction and is the price of making the guarantee falsifiable -- amortised over many deltas but not bounded by any one of them. An O(delta) claim for this project is therefore defensible only in the form: 'incremental cost is proportional to the observed node-tree mutation volume, with the following thirteen named exclusions, one periodic O(page) verification, and a declared-incompleteness flag set whenever an excluded construct is present on the page.'
reanchoring_stability: MutationObserver is the best available signal for CHEAP re-anchoring precisely because it hands you node identity across the change: a childList record carries live references to the added and removed nodes plus previousSibling and nextSibling, so an insertion tells you exactly where in an existing sibling list a new node landed and the surrounding nodes' identities are unchanged. Used this way, an insertion that shifts every following sibling's positional xpath is recognised as a shift rather than as a mass delete-and-recreate, and the addresses can be re-derived arithmetically -- the O(subtree) rekey named as an exception in item 23 is still paid, but no matching or guessing is involved and the result is exact. That is the strongest argument for driving the trie's address maintenance from records rather than from re-derivation. It only holds for changes that produce records; for everything in the blind-spot list, re-anchoring falls back to content-hash matching against a fresh capture, with no record to guide it. No measured re-anchor rate exists for this mechanism because nobody has published one.
adversarial_exposure: MutationObserver reports what the DOM says regardless of visibility, so it preserves hidden content on equal footing with visible content -- consistent with the project's layout-blind position and neither better nor worse than a full DOM read. Three adversarial properties specific to the delta channel are worth stating. (1) A hostile page can HIDE content from the sensor for free by putting it in a closed shadow root, in a canvas, or in CSS generated content, all of which are outside the record stream and outside a DOM-based fold entirely -- so a layout-blind, DOM-based sensor has a well-defined and cheaply exploited blind region that an injection can live in only if the injection also needs to be invisible to the model, which it does not, so this cuts against fidelity more than against safety. (2) A hostile page can BURY a real change by generating enormous record volume -- churning class attributes at frame rate makes the record stream noise-dominated and any per-record processing budget will be exhausted, which is a denial-of-service against the sensor and a way to force a lossy path. Record-rate limiting with an explicit overflow flag is the mitigation, and the flag must be loud. (3) The 58.6%-of-concealed-injections figure for rendering-based concealment (display:none, zero size, off-screen) is exactly the class MutationObserver cannot adjudicate, because it never reads computed style. What IS available inside the fold without geometry is the DOM-level and character-level evidence: the hidden content attribute, aria-hidden, inline style attribute text (which is reported as an attribute record and can be inspected as a STRING without computing layout -- reading 'display:none' out of a style attribute is a string operation, not a geometry read, and is legitimately inside the fold), class names as opaque tokens, tabindex=-1, and the Unicode composition of text. That set covers inline-styled concealment and declarative hiding but not stylesheet-driven concealment, which requires either computed style or CSSOM inspection and therefore sits outside. The honest ceiling for a layout-blind design is: all Unicode-level concealment, all attribute-declared hiding, and inline-style-declared hiding -- with stylesheet-driven and geometry-driven concealment structurally out of reach and needing to be declared as such rather than defended against.
provenance_carrying: Excellent per record and this is under-used. Every MutationRecord names its target node, from which an address is derivable, and the tree it belongs to identifies the shadow depth. Combined with a capture timestamp taken at callback time, each record carries origin, address, time and shadow depth with no extra bookkeeping -- exactly the provenance tuple the injection-defence literature asks for, delivered for free by the change channel. The gap is that a record does not carry the SOURCE of the mutation: there is no indication whether a change came from the page's first-party script, a third-party script, an ad frame's parent-page manipulation, or the user. That distinction is precisely what a provenance-based injection defence wants and the API does not supply it; approximating it requires stack capture inside the callback, which is expensive and unreliable because the callback runs in a microtask after the mutating code has returned, so the stack is gone. Record what IS available -- address, tree, time, record type -- and be explicit that mutation authorship is not obtainable.
roundtrip_safety: The relevant round trip is state-plus-delta versus fresh-capture, and it is the soundness test described under independent_oracle: apply records to the stored fold, capture the page fresh, compare. Equality is a fixed point; inequality names a blind spot with an address. This should be a standing test and it is the single highest-value thing in this item. A second round trip worth having: serialise the record stream, replay it against the stored initial DOM in a fresh context, and check the resulting fold equals the online one -- this validates that the record stream is a sufficient artifact and makes offline reproduction possible. Escaping is not an issue at this layer; records carry raw strings and any escaping policy belongs to the markdown projection.
token_budget_and_ordering: MutationObserver emits no tokens but determines what a change-driven emission can offer. The valuable property is that records give a natural RECENCY ordering and a natural change-scoped subset, so a budgeted update can be 'here is what changed since you last looked, in the order it changed', which is far cheaper than re-emitting a page. Given that position bias becomes recency-dominant past roughly half the context fill, a change-ordered emission is well matched to how the model will actually weight it -- the newest change lands last and is weighted most, which is usually the desired semantics for an interaction result. The countervailing risk is record amplification: emitting one line per record on a framework-driven page floods the budget with no-op class changes, so the delta must be COALESCED to net semantic change (final state per address, no-ops dropped by comparing old and new values) before it is costed. Coalescing by address is cheap, is exactly what a trie keyed by address supports, and turns record count into node count.
representation_cost: A MutationRecord is small: a type string, a target reference, two short node lists, an attribute name, and optionally an old value string. Memory cost is dominated by holding references to removed subtrees, which keeps them alive and can retain large detached trees until the records are released -- a real leak source if records are buffered. Processing cost is dominated by the subtree walks that childList records imply, not by the records themselves. In token terms the API costs nothing directly; the emission built on it costs whatever the coalesced net change costs, which for a well-behaved incremental page is a handful of nodes and for a virtualised list is the visible window.
what_could_be_adopted: Five things. (1) THE PER-SHADOW-ROOT OBSERVER SET as the delta channel's actual architecture: one observer per open shadow root plus the main document, maintained by discovering new hosts from childList records on newly added elements, with a periodic full scan as the correctness backstop for shadow roots attached to pre-existing elements. This is the honest implementation of composed-tree observation without patching anything. (2) SLOTCHANGE LISTENERS alongside the observers, because the composed tree can change with an empty record stream and slotchange is the only signal. Without this the O(delta) claim is simply false for slotted content. (3) attributeFilter RESTRICTED TO THE INTERACTIVITY SET as a hard bound on both cost and noise, with the filtered-out attributes declared. (4) THE PERIODIC FULL-RECAPTURE ORACLE, which is the mechanism that makes the whole guarantee falsifiable and which nothing else in this research set supplies as cleanly. (5) A DECLARED-INCOMPLETENESS FLAG SET computed at capture: closed shadow roots present, canvas present, cross-origin iframes present, declarative shadow DOM detected, CSS generated content in use, record-rate overflow occurred. This is the concrete form of 'naming the exceptions is what makes the guarantee falsifiable'. Explicitly NOT worth adopting: any attempt to reach closed shadow roots (refused by constraint and detectable); transition-abusing style observation as a general mechanism, since it requires naming properties in advance and is a workaround for a missing platform feature; and polling computed style, which reads layout and belongs in the actuator layer if anywhere.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS. The API reports tag- and attribute-level facts with no semantic interpretation and cannot name a region. Care is needed only that the attributeFilter list stays a mechanical interactivity vocabulary (aria-*, disabled, checked, open, hidden, href, tabindex, contenteditable, role, class, style) rather than growing into a hand-tuned per-site rule set, which would smuggle a heuristic in through the back door. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, and it is the cleanest fit in this whole item set -- MutationObserver cannot read geometry even if asked. Its geometric siblings ResizeObserver and IntersectionObserver are ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY. A subtle boundary case worth ruling on explicitly: reading the string 'display:none' out of a style ATTRIBUTE is a string operation on DOM data and is inside the fold; calling getComputedStyle is a layout read and is not. o_delta: ADOPTABLE AS-IS FOR NODE-TREE CHANGE, WITH THIRTEEN NAMED EXCLUSIONS. This is the item that defines the project's O(delta) guarantee, and the guarantee is only falsifiable if the exclusions in delta_cost_model are published alongside it. Two of them -- slot reassignment and declarative shadow DOM in the initial parse -- are genuine soundness holes in a COMPOSED-tree fold specifically, not merely coverage gaps, and both have concrete mitigations (slotchange listeners, initial shadow-root enumeration). no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS and actively supportive: the API only exists in a real browser against a real document, so there is nothing to stub and the measured path is real by construction. The one discipline to keep is that the blind-spot oracle must run against real pages, since synthetic test documents exhibit none of the constructs that cause the blind spots. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: ADOPTABLE AS-IS AND CONSTRAINT-CONFIRMING. MutationObserver respects the closed-root boundary by design; it requires no patching, offers no bypass, and its inability to see closed roots is exactly the behaviour the constraint demands. The right response is to DECLARE closed-root presence in the capture metadata, not to work around it. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is, and it is the load-bearing mechanism for the project's incrementality claim -- provided the exclusion list is treated as part of the specification of that claim rather than as errata.
governance_signal_handling: None, and none is expected -- this is an in-page API, not a fetching mechanism. robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF and HTTP 402 all govern retrieval, and by the time an observer is running the retrieval has already happened. The one indirect relevance is that observing a page implies being on it, and governance decisions must therefore be made before navigation, at the fetch layer, and recorded on the url node where the observed mutations will later hang. Note also that mutation-driven capture of content loaded by the page's own subsequent XHR/fetch calls constitutes retrieval of resources whose own governance signals were never checked, since the sensor sees only the rendered result -- a real gap, and one that is invisible unless network requests are logged alongside mutations.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The API itself processes nothing persistently; the regulated act is what the project stores. Two mutation-specific points. First, a mutation stream captures a page IN USE, including content that appears as a result of the operator's own interactions -- form values typed, search queries entered, authenticated content revealed -- so a mutation log is behaviourally richer and more personally identifying than a static capture of the same URL, and should carry a higher retention sensitivity class. Second, the property blind spot has an ironic privacy upside: because input.value changes generate no records, keystroke-level content typed into forms does not enter the mutation stream by default, and any deliberate move to capture it (polling properties, listening to input events) is a conscious decision to collect exactly the most sensitive category of data. That decision should be explicit, off by default, and separately flagged in the capture metadata. Retention and erasure follow the address scheme rather than the observer. [uncertain] on the specific lawful-basis analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject.
